message.content:
The number of mitochondria in a cell varies widely depending on the cell type and its metabolic demands. In most mammalian cells, you’ll find anywhere from **a few dozen to several thousand mitochondria**. For example:

| Cell type | Typical mitochondrial count (per cell) | Notes |
|-----------|----------------------------------------|-------|
| Neurons (high energy demand) | 10 000–100 000 | Especially in axons and dendrites |
| Muscle cells (skeletal, cardiac) | 10 000–50 000 | Dense network for ATP production |
| Hepatocytes (liver) | 1 000–10 000 | High metabolic activity |
| Epithelial cells (skin, gut) | 100–1 000 | Moderate energy needs |
| Stem cells (low differentiation) | 10–100 | Lower metabolic rate |

So while a typical “average” cell might contain a few hundred mitochondria, specialized cells can have orders of magnitude more.
